entries.97c2ac787487599d48eca71dcbc5320dad8c6f52: <div sID="gen9400" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Job.8" sID="Job.8"/> <div eID="gen9400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9401" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9402" type="x-p"/> Job's friends are like Job's messengers: the latter followed one another close with evil tidings, the former followed him with harsh censures: both, unawares, served Satan's design; these to drive him from his integrity, those to drive him from the comfort of it. Eliphaz did not reply to what Job had said in answer to him, but left it to Bildad, whom he knew to be of the same mind with himself in this affair. Those are not the wisest of the company, but the weakest rather, who covet to have all the talk. Let others speak in their turn, and let the first keep silence, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.30-1Cor.14.31">1 Cor. xiv. 30, 31</reference>. Eliphaz had undertaken to show that because Job was sorely afflicted he was certainly a wicked man. Bildad is much of the same mind, and will conclude Job a wicked man unless God do speedily appear for his relief. In this chapter he endeavours to convince Job, I. That he had spoken too passionately, <reference osisRef="Job.8.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. That he and his children had suffered justly, <reference osisRef="Job.8.3-Job.8.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. That, if he were a true penitent, God would soon turn his captivity, <reference osisRef="Job.8.5-Job.8.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. IV. That it was a usual thing for Providence to extinguish the joys and hopes of wicked men as his were extinguished; and therefore that they had reason to suspect him for a hypocrite, <reference osisRef="Job.8.8-Job.8.19">ver. 8-19</reference>. V. That they would be abundantly confirmed in their suspicion unless God did speedily appear for his relief, <reference osisRef="Job.8.20-Job.8.22">ver. 20-22</reference>.
entries.9b2b8134f190c17079dcd539c1c335957447668f: <div eID="gen9402" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9401" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Bildad. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, 2 How long wilt thou speak these <hi type="italic">things?</hi> and <hi type="italic">how long shall</hi> the words of thy mouth <hi type="italic">be like</hi> a strong wind? 3 Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice? <hi type="super">4</hi> If thy children have sinned against him, and he have cast them away for their transgression; <hi type="super">5</hi> If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty; <hi type="super">6</hi> If thou <hi type="italic">wert</hi> pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous. <hi type="super">7</hi> Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase. <div eID="gen9403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9404" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Bildad reproves Job for what he had said (<reference osisRef="Job.8.2">v. 2</reference>), checks his passion, but perhaps (as is too common) with greater passion. We thought Job spoke a great deal of good sense and much to the purpose, and that he had reason and right on his side; but Bildad, like an eager angry disputant, turns it all off with this, <hi type="italic">How long wilt thou speak these things?</hi> taking it for granted that Eliphaz had said enough to silence him, and that therefore all he said was impertinent. Thus (as Caryl observes) reproofs are often grounded upon mistakes. Men's meaning is not taken aright, and then they are gravely rebuked as if they were evil-doers. Bildad compares Job's discourse to a <hi type="italic">strong wind.</hi> Job had excused himself with this, that his speeches were but <hi type="italic">as wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.6.26">ch. vi. 26</reference>), and therefore they should not make such ado about them: "Yea, but" (says Bildad) "they are as strong wind, blustering and threatening, boisterous and dangerous, and therefore we are concerned to fence against them." <div eID="gen9404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9405" type="x-p"/> II. He justifies God in what he had done. This he had no occasion to do at this time (for Job did not condemn God, as he would have it thought he did), or he might at least have done it without reflecting upon Job's children, as he does here. Could he not be an advocate for God but he must be an accuser of the brethren? 1. He is right in general, that <hi type="italic">God doth not pervert judgment,</hi> nor ever go contrary to any settled rule of justice, <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">v. 3</reference>. Far be it from him that he should and from us that we should suspect him. He never oppresses the innocent, nor lays a greater load on the guilty than they deserve. He is God, the Judge; and shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? <reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">Gen. xviii. 25</reference>. If there should be unrighteousness with God, <hi type="italic">how should he judge the world?</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5-Rom.3.6">Rom. iii. 5, 6</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">Almighty, Shaddai—all sufficient.</hi> Men pervert justice sometimes for fear of the power of others (but God is Almighty, and stands in awe of none), sometimes to obtain the favour of others; but God is all-sufficient, and cannot be benefited by the favour of any. It is man's weakness and impotency that he often is unjust; it is God's omnipotence that he cannot be so. 2. Yet he is not fair and candid in the application. He takes it for granted that Job's children (the death of whom was one of the greatest of his afflictions) had been guilty of some notorious wickedness, and that the unhappy circumstances of their death were sufficient evidence that they were sinners above all the children of the east, <reference osisRef="Job.8.4">v. 4</reference>. Job readily owned that God did not pervert judgment; and yet it did not therefore follow either that his children were cast-aways or that they died for some great transgression. It is true that we and our children have sinned against God, and we ought to justify him in all he brings upon us and ours; but extraordinary afflictions are not always the punishment of extraordinary sins, but sometimes the trial of extraordinary graces; and, in our judgment of another's case (unless the contrary appears), we ought to take the more favourable side, as our Saviour directs, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.2-Luke.13.4">Luke xiii. 2-4</reference>. Here Bildad missed it. <div eID="gen9405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9406" type="x-p"/> III. He put Job in hope that, if he were indeed upright, as he said he was, he should yet see a good issue of his present troubles: "<hi type="italic">Although thy children have sinned against him, and are cast away in their transgression</hi> (they have died in their own sin), yet if thou be pure and upright thyself, and as an evidence of that wilt now seek unto God and submit to him, all shall be well yet," <reference osisRef="Job.8.5-Job.8.7">v. 5-7</reference>. This may be taken two ways, either, 1. As designed to prove Job a hypocrite and a wicked man, though not by the greatness, yet the by the continuance, of his afflictions. "When thou wast impoverished, and thy children were killed, if thou hadst been pure and upright, and approved thyself so in the trial, God would before now have returned in mercy to thee and comforted thee according to the time of thy affliction; but, because he does not so, we have reason to conclude thou art not so <hi type="italic">pure and upright</hi> as thou pretendest to be. If thou hadst conducted thyself well under the former affliction, thou wouldst not have been struck with the latter." Herein Bildad was not in the right; for a good man may be afflicted for his trial, not only very sorely, but very long, and yet, if for life, it is in comparison with eternity but for a moment. But, since Bildad put it to this issue, God was pleased to join issue with him, and proved his servant Job an honest man by Bildad's own argument; for, soon after, he blessed his latter end more than his beginning. Or, 2. As designed to direct and encourage Job, that he might not thus run himself into despair, and give up all for gone; there might yet be hope if he would take the right course. I am apt to think Bildad here intended to condemn Job, yet would be thought to counsel and comfort him. (1.) He gives him good counsel, yet perhaps not expecting he would take it, the same that Eliphaz had given him (<reference osisRef="Job.5.8">ch. v. 8</reference>), to <hi type="italic">seek unto God,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">betimes</hi> (that is, speedily and seriously), and not to be dilatory and trifling in his return and repentance. He advises him not to complain, but to petition, to <hi type="italic">make</hi> his <hi type="italic">supplication to the Almighty</hi> with humility and faith, and to see that there was (what he feared had hitherto been wanting) sincerity in his heart ("thou must be <hi type="italic">pure and upright</hi>") and honesty in his house—"that must be <hi type="italic">the habitation of thy righteousness,</hi> and not filled with ill-gotten goods, else God will not hear thy prayers," <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>. It is only the prayer of the upright that is the acceptable and prevailing prayer, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Prov. xv. 8</reference>. (2.) He gives him good hopes that he shall yet again see good days, secretly suspecting, however, that he was not qualified to see them. He assures him that, if he would be early in seeking God, God would awake for his relief, would remember him and return to him, though now he seemed to forget him and forsake him—that if his habitation were righteous it should be prosperity. When we return to God in a way of duty we have reason to hope that he will return to us in a way of mercy. Let not Job object that he had so little left to being the world with again that it was impossible he should ever prosper as he had done; no, "Though thy beginning should be ever so small, a little meal in the barrel and a little oil in the cruse, God's blessing shall multiply that to a great increase." This is God's way of enriching the souls of his people with graces and comforts, not <hi type="italic">per saltum—as by a bound,</hi> but <hi type="italic">per gradum—step by step.</hi> The beginning is small, but the progress is to perfection. Dawning light grows to noonday, a grain of mustard seed to a great tree. Let us not therefore despise the day of small things, but hope for the day of great things.
entries.266cc9d6220477dca14936743d1f1c186545b24d: <div eID="gen9406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9407" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers: <hi type="super">9</hi> (For we <hi type="italic">are but of</hi> yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth <hi type="italic">are</hi> a shadow:) <hi type="super">10</hi> Shall not they teach thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> tell thee, and utter words out of their heart? 11 Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water? <hi type="super">12</hi> Whilst it <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet in his greenness, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not cut down, it withereth before any <hi type="italic">other</hi> herb. 13 So <hi type="italic">are</hi> the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish: <hi type="super">14</hi> Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a spider's web. <hi type="super">15</hi> He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure. <hi type="super">16</hi> He <hi type="italic">is</hi> green before the sun, and his branch shooteth forth in his garden. <hi type="super">17</hi> His roots are wrapped about the heap, <hi type="italic">and</hi> seeth the place of stones. <hi type="super">18</hi> If he destroy him from his place, then <hi type="italic">it</hi> shall deny him, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> I have not seen thee. <hi type="super">19</hi> Behold, this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall others grow. <div eID="gen9407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9408" type="x-p"/> Bildad here discourses very well on the sad catastrophe of hypocrites and evil-doers and the fatal period of all their hopes and joys. He will not be so bold as to say with Eliphaz that none that were righteous were ever cut off thus (<reference osisRef="Job.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>); yet he takes it for granted that God, in the course of his providence, does ordinarily bring wicked men, who seemed pious and were prosperous, to shame and ruin in this world, and that, by making their prosperity short, he discovers their piety to be counterfeit. Whether this will certainly prove that all who are thus ruined must be concluded to have been hypocrites he will not say, but rather suspect, and thinks the application is easy. <div eID="gen9408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9409" type="x-p"/> I. He proves this truth, of the certain destruction of all the hopes and joys of hypocrites, by an appeal to antiquity and the concurring sentiment and observation of all wise and good men; and an undoubted truth it is, if we take in the other world, that, if not in this life, yet in the life to come, hypocrites will be deprived of all their trusts and all their triumphs: whether Bildad so meant or no, we must so take it. Let us observe the method of his proof, <reference osisRef="Job.8.8-Job.8.10">v. 8-10</reference>. <div eID="gen9409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9410" type="x-p"/> 1. He insists not on his own judgment and that of his companions: <hi type="italic">We are but of yesterday, and know nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">v. 9</reference>. He perceived that Job had no opinion of their abilities, but thought they knew little. "We will own," says Bildad, "that we know nothing, are as ready to confess our ignorance as thou art to condemn it; for we are but of yesterday in comparison, <hi type="italic">and our days upon earth are</hi> short and transient, and hastening away as <hi type="italic">a shadow.</hi> And hence," (1.) "We are not so near the fountain-head of divine revelation" (which then for aught that appears, was conveyed by tradition) "as the former age was; and therefore we must enquire what they said and recount what we have been told of their sentiments." Blessed be God, now that we have the word of God in writing, and are directed to search that, we need not <hi type="italic">enquire of the former age,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">prepare ourselves to the search of their fathers;</hi> for, though we ourselves are but of yesterday, the word of God in the scripture is as nigh to us as it was to them (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">Rom. x. 8</reference>), and it is the <hi type="italic">more sure word of prophecy, to which we must take heed.</hi> If we study and keep God's precepts, we may by them <hi type="italic">understand more than the ancients,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99-Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 99, 100</reference>. (2.) "We do not live so long as those of the former age did, to make observations upon the methods of divine providence, and therefore cannot be such competent judges as they in a cause of this nature." Note, The shortness of our lives is a great hindrance to the improvement of our knowledge, and so are the frailty and weakness of our bodies. <hi type="italic">Vita brevis, ars longa—life is short, the progress of art boundless.</hi> <div eID="gen9410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9411" type="x-p"/> 2. He refers to the testimony of the ancients and to the knowledge which Job himself had of their sentiments. "Do thou <hi type="italic">enquire of the former age,</hi> and let them tell thee, not only their own judgment in this matter, but the judgment also of <hi type="italic">their fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.8">v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">They will teach thee,</hi> and inform thee (<reference osisRef="Job.8.10">v. 10</reference>), that all along, in their time, the judgments of God followed wicked men. This they will <hi type="italic">utter out of their hearts,</hi> that is, as that which they firmly believe themselves, which they are greatly affected with and desirous to acquaint and affect others with." Note, (1.) For the right understanding of divine Providence, and the unfolding of the difficulties of it, it will be of use to compare the observations and experiences of former ages with the events of our own day; and, in order thereto, to consult history, especially the sacred history, which is the most ancient, infallibly true, and written designedly for our learning. (2.) Those that would fetch knowledge from the former ages must search diligently, <hi type="italic">prepare for the search,</hi> and take pains for the search. (3.) Those words are most likely to reach to the hearts of the learners that come from the hearts of the teachers. <hi type="italic">Those shall teach thee</hi> best that <hi type="italic">utter words out of their heart,</hi> that speak by experience, and not by rote, of spiritual and divine things. The learned bishop Patrick suggests that Bildad being a Shuhite, descended from Shuah one of Abraham's sons by Keturah (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.2">Gen. xxv. 2</reference>), in this appeal which he makes to history he has a particular respect to the rewards which the blessing of God secured to the posterity of faithful Abraham (who hitherto, and long after, continued in his religion) and to the extirpation of those eastern people, neighbours to Job (in whose country they were settled), for their wickedness, whence he infers that it is God's usual way to prosper the just and root out the wicked, though for a while they may flourish. <div eID="gen9411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9412" type="x-p"/> II. He illustrates this truth by some similitudes. <div eID="gen9412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9413" type="x-p"/> 1. The hopes and joys of the hypocrite are here compared to a rush or flag, <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.13">v. 11-13</reference>. (1.) It grows up out of the mire and water. The hypocrite cannot gain his hope without some false rotten ground or other out of which to raise it, and with which to support it and keep it alive, any more than the rush can grow without mire. He grounds it on his worldly prosperity, the plausible profession he makes of religion, the good opinion of his neighbours, and his own good conceit of himself, which are no solid foundation on which to build his confidence. It is all but mire and water; and the hope that grows out of it is but rush and flag. (2.) It may look green and gay for a while (the rush outgrows the grass), but it is light and hollow, and empty, and good for nothing. It is green for show, but of no use. (3.) It withers presently, <hi type="italic">before any other herb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.12">v. 12</reference>. Even <hi type="italic">while it is in its greenness</hi> it is dried away and gone in a little time. Note, The best state of hypocrites and evil-doers borders upon withering; even when it is green it is going. The grass is <hi type="italic">cut down and withers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">Ps. xc. 6</reference>); but the rush is <hi type="italic">not cut down</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">withers, withers before it grows up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.129.6">Ps. cxxix. 6</reference>): as it has no use, so it has no continuance. <hi type="italic">So are the paths of all that forget God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.13">v. 13</reference>); they take the same way that the rush does, <hi type="italic">for the hypocrite's hope shall perish.</hi> Note, [1.] Forgetfulness of God is at the bottom of men's hypocrisy, and of the vain hopes with which they flatter and deceive themselves in their hypocrisy. Men would not be hypocrites if they did not forget that the God with whom they have to do searches the heart and requires truth there, that he is a Spirit and has his eye on our spirits; and hypocrites would have no hope if they did not forget that God is righteous, and will not be mocked with the torn and the lame. [2.] The hope of hypocrites is a great cheat upon themselves, and, though it may flourish for a while, it will certainly perish at last, and they with it. <div eID="gen9413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9414" type="x-p"/> 2. They are here compared <hi type="italic">to a spider's web,</hi> or <hi type="italic">a spider's house</hi> (as it is in the margin), a cobweb, <reference osisRef="Job.8.14-Job.8.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. The hope of the hypocrite, (1.) Is woven out of his own bowels; it is the creature of his own fancy, and arises merely from a conceit of his own merit and sufficiency. There is a great deal of difference between the work of the bee and that of the spider. A diligent Christian, like the laborious bee, fetches in all his comfort from the heavenly dews of God's word; but the hypocrite, like the subtle spider, weaves his out of a false hypothesis of his own concerning God, as if he were altogether such a one as himself. (2.) He is very fond of it, as the spider of her web; pleases himself with it, wraps himself in it, calls it his house, <hi type="italic">leans upon it,</hi> and <hi type="italic">holds it fast.</hi> It is said of the spider that <hi type="italic">she takes hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.28">Prov. xxx. 28</reference>. So does a carnal worldling hug himself in the fulness and firmness of his outward prosperity; he prides himself in that house as his palace, fortifies himself in it as his castle, and makes use of it as the spider of her web, to ensnare those he has a mind to prey upon. So does a formal professor; he flatters himself in his own eyes, doubts not of his salvation, is secure of heaven, and cheats the world with his vain confidences. (3.) It will easily and certainly be swept away, as the cobweb with the besom, when God shall come to purge his house. The prosperity of worldly people will fail them when they expect to find safety and happiness in it. They seek to hold fast their estates, but God is plucking them out of their hands; and whose shall all those things be, which they have provided? or what the better they will be for them? The confidences of hypocrites will fail them. <hi type="italic">I tell you, I know you not.</hi> The house built on the sand will fall in the storm, when the builder most needs it and promised himself the benefit of it. <hi type="italic">When a wicked man dies his expectation perishes.</hi> The ground of his hopes will prove false; he will be disappointed of the thing he hoped for, and his foolish hope with which he buoyed himself up will be turned into endless despair; and thus his hope will be cut off, his web, that refuge of lies, swept away, and he crushed in it. <div eID="gen9414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9415" type="x-p"/> 3. The hypocrite is here compared to a flourishing and well-rooted tree, which, though it do not wither of itself, yet will easily be cut down and its place know it no more. The secure and prosperous sinner may think himself wronged when he is compared to a rush and a flag; he thinks he has a better root. "We will allow him his conceit," says Bildad, "and give him all the advantage he can desire, and bring him in suddenly cut off." He is here represented as Nebuchadnezzar was in his own dream (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.10">Dan. iv. 10</reference>) by a great tree. (1.) See this tree fair and flourishing (<reference osisRef="Job.8.16">v. 16</reference>) like a <hi type="italic">green bay-tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">Ps. xxxvii. 35</reference>), <hi type="italic">green before the sun,</hi> it keeps its greenness in defiance of the scorching sun-beams, and <hi type="italic">his branch shoots forth</hi> under the protection of his garden-wall and with the benefit of his garden-soil. See it fixed, and taking deep root, never likely to be overthrown by stormy winds, <hi type="italic">for his roots are interwoven with the stones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.17">v. 17</reference>); it grows in firm ground, not, as the rush, of mire and water. Thus does a wicked man, when he prospers in the world, think himself secure; his wealth is a <hi type="italic">high wall in his own conceit.</hi> (2.) See this tree felled and forgotten notwithstanding, <hi type="italic">destroyed from his place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.18">v. 18</reference>), and so entirely extirpated that there shall remain no sign or token where it grew. The very place say, <hi type="italic">I have not seen thee;</hi> and the standers by shall say the same. <hi type="italic">I sought him, but he could not be found,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.36.36">Ps. xxxvi. 36</reference>. He made a great show and a great noise for a time, but he is gone of a sudden, and <hi type="italic">neither root nor branch is left him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">This is the joy</hi> (that is, this is the end and conclusion) <hi type="italic">of the wicked man's way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.19">v. 19</reference>); this is that which all his joy comes to. <hi type="italic">The way of the ungodly shall perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>. His hope, he thought, would in the issue be turned into joy; but this is the issue, this is the joy. <hi type="italic">The harvest shall be a heap in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.17.11">Isa. xvii. 11</reference>. This is the best of it; and what then is the worst of it? But shall he not leave a family behind him to enjoy what he has? No, <hi type="italic">out of the earth</hi> (not out of his roots) <hi type="italic">shall others grow,</hi> that are nothing akin to him, and shall fill up his place, and rule over that for which he labored. Others (that is, others of the same spirit and disposition) shall grow up in his place, and be as secure as ever he was, not warned by his fall. The way of worldlings is their folly, and yet there is a race of those that <hi type="italic">approve their sayings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Ps. xlix. 13</reference>.
entries.9db0c81e8750eb15e90451057e9f561ffa5ce465: <div eID="gen9415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9416" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Behold, God will not cast away a perfect <hi type="italic">man,</hi> neither will he help the evil doers: <hi type="super">21</hi> Till he fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing. <hi type="super">22</hi> They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame; and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought. <div eID="gen9416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9417" type="x-p"/> Bildad here, in the close of his discourse, sums up what he has to say in a few words, setting before Job life and death, the blessing and the curse, assuring him that as he was so he should fare, and therefore they might conclude that as he fared so he was. 1. On the one hand, if he were a perfect upright man, God would not <hi type="italic">cast him away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.20">v. 20</reference>. Though now he seemed forsaken of God, he would yet return to him, and by degrees would <hi type="italic">turn his mourning into dancing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.11">Ps. xxx. 11</reference>) and comforts should flow in upon him so plentifully that his <hi type="italic">mouth</hi> should be <hi type="italic">filled with laughing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.21">v. 21</reference>. So affecting should the happy change be, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.2">Ps. cxxvi. 2</reference>. Those that loved him would rejoice with him; but those that hated him, and had triumphed in his fall, would be ashamed of their insolence, when they should see him restored to his former prosperity. Now it is true that <hi type="italic">God will not cast away an upright man;</hi> he may be cast down for a time, but he shall not be cast away for ever. It is true that, if not in this world, yet in another, the mouth of the righteous shall be <hi type="italic">filled with rejoicing.</hi> Though their sun should set under a cloud, yet it shall rise again clear, never more to be clouded; though they go mourning to the grave, that shall not hinder their entrance into the joy of their Lord. It is true that the enemies of the saints will be <hi type="italic">clothed with shame</hi> when they see them crowned with honour. But it does not therefore follow that, if Job were not perfectly restored to his former prosperity, he would forfeit the character of a perfect man. 2. On the other hand, if he were a wicked man and an evil-doer, God would not help him, but leave him to perish in his present distresses (<reference osisRef="Job.8.20">v. 20</reference>), and his <hi type="italic">dwelling-place</hi> should <hi type="italic">come to nought,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.8.22">v. 22</reference>. And here also it is true that God <hi type="italic">will not help the evil-doers;</hi> they throw themselves out of his protection, and forfeit his favour. He <hi type="italic">will not take the ungodly by the hand</hi> (so it is in the margin), will not have fellowship and communion with them; for <hi type="italic">what communion</hi> can there be <hi type="italic">between light and darkness?</hi> He will not lend them his hand to pull them out of the miseries, the eternal miseries, into which they have plunged themselves; they will then stretch out their hand to him for help, but it will be too late: he will not take them by the hand. <hi type="italic">Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed.</hi> It is true that <hi type="italic">the dwelling-place of the wicked,</hi> sooner or later, <hi type="italic">will come to nought.</hi> Those only <hi type="italic">who make God their dwelling-place</hi> are safe for ever, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Ps. xc. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">xci. 1</reference>. Those who make other things their refuge will be disappointed. Sin brings ruin on persons and families. Yet to argue (as Bildad, I doubt, slyly does) that because Job's family was sunk, and he himself at present seemed helpless, therefore he certainly was an ungodly wicked man, was neither just nor charitable, as long as there appeared no other evidence of his wickedness and ungodliness. Let us <hi type="italic">judge nothing before the time,</hi> but wait till the secrets of all hearts shall be made manifest, and the present difficulties of Providence be solved to universal and everlasting satisfaction, when the <hi type="italic">mystery of God shall be finished.</hi>  <chapter eID="Job.8"/> <div eID="gen9417" type="x-p"/>

entries.d24953c282a877fc16175d8800d3de6c3c1eebd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4602"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen6672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">FIRST SERIES--</hi>FIRST SPEECH OF BILDAD, MORE SEVERE AND COARSE THAN THAT OF ELIPHAZ.<div eID="gen6672" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.8.1-Job.8.22">Job 8:1-22</reference>. The Address of Bildad.</title> <div sID="gen6673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4602"/><hi type="bold">2. like a ... wind?--</hi>disregarding restraints, and daring against God. <div eID="gen6673" type="x-p"/>
entries.0851ecf32575137a6d5588e83e662d1716204198: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4603"/><div sID="gen6674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4603"/>3. The repetition of "pervert" gives an emphasis galling to Job (<reference osisRef="Job.34.12">Job 34:12</reference>). "Wouldst thou have God," as thy words imply, "pervert judgment," by letting thy sins go unpunished? He assumes Job's guilt from his sufferings. <div eID="gen6674" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bcdfd5706d7c27320ddccf41a274911f96147a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4604"/><div sID="gen6675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4604"/><hi type="bold">4. If--</hi>Rather, "Since thy children have sinned against Him, and (since) He has cast them away (Hebrew, by the hand of) for their transgressions, (yet) if thou wouldst seek unto God, &c., if thou wert pure, &c., surely [even] now He would awake for thee." Umbreit makes the apodosis to, "since thy children," &c., begin at "He has cast them away." Also, instead of "for," "He gave them up to (literally, into the hand of) their own guilt." Bildad expresses the justice of God, which Job had arraigned. Thy children have sinned; God leaves them to the consequence of their sin; most cutting to the heart of the bereaved father. <div eID="gen6675" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfe1c707e9d3216eb2d03af9bdb986f76d6706e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4605"/><div sID="gen6676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4605"/><hi type="bold">5. seek unto God betimes--</hi>early. Make it the first and chief anxiety (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.34">Psa 78:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.5.15">Ho 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Is 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">Pr 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.24">13:24</reference>). <div eID="gen6676" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7ae4526492027de9521a016d9baa060bb5b3571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4606"/><div sID="gen6677" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4606"/><hi type="bold">6. He would awake for thee--</hi>that is, arise to thy help. God seemed to be asleep toward the sufferer (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.23">Psa 35:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Is 51:9</reference>).<div eID="gen6677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make ... prosperous--</hi>restore to prosperity thy (their) righteous habitation. Bildad assumes it to have been heretofore the habitation of guilt. <div eID="gen6678" type="x-p"/>
entries.d580e525da62edda06807a93deced306207f6ae2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4607"/><div sID="gen6679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4607"/><hi type="bold">7. thy beginning--</hi>the beginning of thy new happiness after restoration.<div eID="gen6679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">latter end--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.42.12">Job 42:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">Pr 23:18</reference>). <div eID="gen6680" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cddca351f21ee38eb804fbbc682f0f1eaf7c318: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4608"/><div sID="gen6681" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4608"/>8-9. The sages of the olden time reached an age beyond those of Job's time (see on <reference osisRef="Job.42.16">Job 42:16</reference>), and therefore could give the testimony of a fuller experience. <div eID="gen6681" type="x-p"/>
entries.db5bfb169d1a7671527075a7e2bdd61c58c0a860: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4610"/><div sID="gen6684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4610"/><hi type="bold">10. teach thee--</hi><reference osisRef="Job.6.24">Job 6:24</reference> had said, "Teach me." Bildad, therefore, says, "Since you want teaching, inquire of the fathers. They will teach thee."<div eID="gen6684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">utter words--</hi>more than mere speaking; "put forth well-considered words."<div eID="gen6685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of their heart--</hi>from observation and reflection; not merely, from their mouth: such, as Bildad insinuates, were Job's words. <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.13">Job 8:11-13</reference> embody in poetic and sententious form (probably the fragment of an old poem) the observation of the elders. The double point of comparison between the ungodly and the paper-reed is: 1. the luxuriant prosperity at first; and, 2. the sudden destruction. <div eID="gen6686" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebb4f470ff2b7d314182e1b6dbbda6ace0c94b52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4611"/><div sID="gen6687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4611"/><hi type="bold">11. rush--</hi>rather, "paper-reed": The papyrus of Egypt, which was used to make garments, shoes, baskets, boats, and paper (a word derived from it). It and the flag, or bulrush, grow only in marshy places (such as are along the Nile). So the godless thrives only in external prosperity; there is in the hypocrite no inward stability; his prosperity is like the rapid growth of water plants. <div eID="gen6687" type="x-p"/>
entries.83f11c3feb9c7854813e3c55f06724146a3dc917: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4612"/><div sID="gen6688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4612"/><hi type="bold">12. not cut down--</hi>Before it has ripened for the scythe, it withers more suddenly than any herb, having no self-sustaining power, once that the moisture is gone, which other herbs do not need in the same degree. So ruin seizes on the godless in the zenith of prosperity, more suddenly than on others who appear less firmly seated in their possessions [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Psa 112:10</reference>). <div eID="gen6688" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff001fcbc50486a608d40e8c810a34744fc5a976: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4613"/><div sID="gen6689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4613"/><hi type="bold">13. paths--</hi>so "ways" (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.19">Pr 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen6689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that forget God--</hi>the distinguishing trait of the godless (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.22">50:22</reference>). <div eID="gen6690" type="x-p"/>
entries.b683f0c70f42c3439e20108d937ad32d4918a0b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4614"/><div sID="gen6691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4614"/><hi type="bold">14. cut off--</hi>so Gesenius; or, to accord with the metaphor of the spider's "house," "The confidence (on which he builds) shall be laid in ruins" (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Is 59:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen6691" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2783214cace1e967892a5b3ba2f59a987c32e5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4615"/><div sID="gen6692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4615"/><hi type="bold">15. he shall hold it fast--</hi>implying his eager grasp, when the storm of trial comes: as the spider "holds fast" by its web; but with this difference: the light spider is sustained by that on which it rests; the godless is not by the thin web on which he rests. The expression, "Hold fast," properly applies to the spider holding his web, but is transferred to the man. Hypocrisy, like the spider's web, is fine-spun, flimsy, and woven out of its own inventions, as the spider's web out of its own bowels. An Arab proverb says, "Time destroys the well-built house, as well as the spider's web." <div eID="gen6692" type="x-p"/>
entries.84a2f339c1564515947b934a5ce4c7b142721a2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4616"/><div sID="gen6693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4616"/><hi type="bold">16. before the sun--</hi>that is, he (the godless) is green only before the sun rises; but he cannot bear its heat, and withers. So succulent plants like the gourd (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.7">Jon 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.8">8</reference>). But the widespreading in the garden does not quite accord with this. Better, "in sunshine"; the sun representing the smiling fortune of the hypocrite, during which he wondrously progresses [Umbreit]. The image is that of weeds growing in rank luxuriance and spreading over even heaps of stones and walls, and then being speedily torn away. <div eID="gen6693" type="x-p"/>
entries.7023ee105f3faf6ac2678621dfffd91b6b0d0c48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4617"/><div sID="gen6694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4617"/><hi type="bold">17. seeth the place of stones--</hi>Hebrew, "the house of stones"; that is, the wall surrounding the garden. The parasite plant, in creeping towards and over the wall--the utmost bound of the garden--is said figuratively to "see" or regard it. <div eID="gen6694" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcd9a27485c5b8b67f40d6b2311afe8b66e1e97d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4618"/><div sID="gen6695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4618"/>18. If He (God) tear him away (properly, "to tear away rapidly and violently") from his place, "then it [the place personified] shall deny him" (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>). The very soil is ashamed of the weeds lying withered on its surface, as though it never had been connected with them. So, when the godless falls from prosperity, his nearest friends disown him. <div eID="gen6695" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2ed45051a8cc18764000632a45fc01368b2dda0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4619"/><div sID="gen6696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4619"/>19. Bitter irony. The hypocrite boasts of joy. This then is his "joy" at the last.<div eID="gen6696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6697" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and out of the earth--</hi>others immediately, who take the place of the man thus punished; not godly men (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.9">Mt 3:9</reference>). For the place of the weeds is among stones, where the gardener wishes no plants. But, ungodly; a fresh crop of weeds always springs up in the place of those torn up: there is no end of hypocrites on earth [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6697" type="x-p"/>
entries.1438934cf1b0ff94cb2985a235f19e3bf6f8a2c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4620"/><div sID="gen6698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4620"/>20. Bildad regards Job as a righteous man, who has fallen into sin.<div eID="gen6698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God will not cast away a perfect man--</hi>(or godly man, such as Job was), if he will only repent. Those alone who persevere in sin God will not help (Hebrew, "take by the hand," <reference osisRef="Ps.73.23">Psa 73:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.13">Is 41:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.6">42:6</reference>) when fallen. <div eID="gen6699" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a85651bb9b429b03566679814233265aa7def20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4621"/><div sID="gen6700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4621"/><hi type="bold">21. Till--</hi>literally, "to the point that"; God's blessing on thee, when repentant, will go on increasing to the point that, or until, &c. <div eID="gen6700" type="x-p"/>
entries.01b0214b40004aa2d5f9ec872d39df66e4b2f1ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4622"/><div sID="gen6701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4622"/>22. The haters of Job are the wicked. They shall be clothed with shame (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.25">Jr 3:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.26">Psa 35:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.29">109:29</reference>), at the failure of their hope that Job would utterly perish, and because they, instead of him, come to naught. <chapter eID="Job.8"/>

entries.2ca091f80061d32c008e6d260660a94d9d599f13: <div eID="gen16191" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16192" type="x-p"/> Bildad answers, and reproves Job for his justifying himself, <reference osisRef="Job.8.1">Job 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.2">Job 8:2</reference>. Shows that God is just, and never punishes but for iniquity; and intimates that it was on account of their sins that his children were cut off, <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.4">Job 8:4</reference>. States that, if Job would humble himself to the Almighty, provided he were innocent, his captivity would soon be turned, and his latter end be abundantly prosperous, <reference osisRef="Job.8.5-Job.8.7">Job 8:5-7</reference>. Appeals to the ancients for the truth of what he says; and draws examples from the vegetable world, to show how soon the wicked may be cut off, and the hope of the hypocrite perish, <reference osisRef="Job.8.8-Job.8.19">Job 8:8-19</reference>. Asserts that God never did cast off a perfect man nor help the wicked; and that, if Job be innocent, his end shall be crowned with prosperity, <reference osisRef="Job.8.20-Job.8.22">Job 8:20-22</reference>. <div eID="gen16192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16193" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16194" type="x-p"/> Bildad the Shuhite - Supposed to be a descendant of Shuah, one of the sons of Abraham, by Keturah, who dwelt in Arabia Deserta, called in Scripture the east country. See <reference osisRef="Gen.25.1">Gen 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.2">Gen 25:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.6">Gen 25:6</reference>.
entries.35ffcebf3c752e453b88dba6c81169eda9c6ebc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16195" type="x-p"/> How long wilt thou speak these things? - Wilt thou still go on to charge God foolishly? Thy heavy affliction proves that thou art under his wrath; and his wrath, thus manifested, proves that it is for thy sins that he punisheth thee. <div eID="gen16195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16196" type="x-p"/> Be like a strong wind? - The Arabic, with which the Syriac agrees, is (Syriac) rucholazomati, the spirit of pride. Wilt thou continue to breathe forth a tempest of words? This is more literal.
entries.10a1ea4e3aa9bc3d406690d096f87fef0928fe7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16197" type="x-p"/> Doth God pervert judgment! - God afflicts thee; can he afflict thee for naught? As he is just, his judgment is just; and he could not inflict punishment unless there be a cause.
entries.521db9a5e2e2cca71ff0b5c6cfb6b2886b3cb095: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16198" type="x-p"/> If thy children have sinned - I know thy children have been cut off by a terrible judgment; but was it not because by transgression they had filled up the measure of their iniquity? <div eID="gen16198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16199" type="x-p"/> And he have cast them away - Has sent them off, says the Targum, to the place of their transgression - to that punishment due to their sins.
entries.9927a346a08f1008da5dc7ce6fabca18ee609858: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16200" type="x-p"/> If thou wouldest seek unto God - Though God has so severely afflicted thee, and removed thy children by a terrible judgment; yet if thou wilt now humble thyself before him, and implore his mercy, thou shalt be saved. He cut them off in their sins, but he spares thee; and this is a proof that he waits to be gracious to thee.
entries.c54986fc0530a4f9038efc5c13f2cc8eff66ddeb: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16201" type="x-p"/> If thou wert pure and upright - Concerning thy guilt there can be no doubt; for if thou hadst been a holy man, and these calamities had occurred through accident, or merely by the malice of thy enemies, would not God, long ere this, have manifested his power and justice in thy behalf, punished thy enemies, and restored thee to affluence? <div eID="gen16201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16202" type="x-p"/> The habitation of thy righteousness - Strongly ironical. If thy house had been as a temple of God, in which his worship had been performed, and his commandments obeyed, would it now be in a state of ruin and desolation?
entries.851b140d35f64c6ec163a490bdecce19988a0e89: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16203" type="x-p"/> Though thy beginning was small - Thy former state, compared to that into which God would have brought thee, would be small; for to show his respect for thy piety, because thou hadst, through thy faithful attachment to him, suffered the loss of all things, he would have greatly multiplied thy former prosperity, so that thou shouldest now have vastly more than thou didst ever before possess.
entries.61eeb8820b2e5c8a165f6d55c89a2fb9efe66f06: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16204" type="x-p"/> Inquire - of the former age - לדור רישון ledor rishon, of the first age; of the patriarchs; the first generation of men that dwelt upon the earth: not of the age that was just past, as Mr. Peters and several others have imagined, in order to keep up the presumption of Job's high antiquity. Bildad most evidently refers to an antiquity exceedingly remote.
entries.6d75c440b19e5e2018a4e27109496e6d1609dfcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16205" type="x-p"/> For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing - It is evident that Bildad refers to those times in which human life was protracted to a much longer date than that in which Job lived; when men, from the long period of eight or nine hundred years, had the opportunity of making many observations, and treasuring up a vast fund of knowledge and experience. In comparison with them, he considers that age as nothing, and that generation as being only of yesterday, not having had opportunity of laying up knowledge: nor could they expect it, as their days upon earth would be but a shadow, compared with that substantial time in which the fathers had lived. Perhaps there may be an allusion here to the shadow projected by the gnomon of a dial, during the time the sun is above the horizon. As is a single solar day, so is our life. The following beautiful motto I have seen on a sundial: Umbrae Sumus! "We are shadows!" referring to the different shadows by which the gnomon marked the hours, during the course of the day; and all intended to convey this moral lesson to the passengers: Your life is composed of time, marked out by such shadows as these. Such as time is, such are you; as fleeting, as transitory, as unsubstantial. These shadows lost, time is lost; time lost, soul lost! Reader take heed! The writer of this book probably had before his eyes these words of David, in his last prayer, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.15">1Chr 29:15</reference> : "For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as all our fathers were; our days upon earth are as a Shadow, and there is no expectation. There is no reason to hope that they shall be prolonged; for our lives are limited down to threescore years and ten, as the average of the life even of old men.
entries.6f26e0af7736fe998c8991f936f3432653f05b64: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16206" type="x-p"/> Shall not they teach thee - Wilt thou not treat their maxims with the utmost deference and respect? They utter words from their heart - what they say is the fruit of long and careful experience.
entries.eaf0d30fbffb0b6d00d0d89ec4c57194b2396461: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> Can the rush grow - The word גמא gome, which we translate rush, is, without doubt, the Egyptian flag papyrus, on which the ancients wrote, and from which our paper derives its name. The Septuagint, who made their Greek translation in Egypt, (if this book made a part of it), and knew well the import of each word in both languages, render גמא gome by παπυρος papyrus, thus: Μη θαλλει παπυρος ανευ ὑδατος; Can the Papyrus flourish without water? Their translation leaves no doubt concerning the meaning of the original. They were probably writing on the very substance in question, while making their translation. The technical language of no science is so thoroughly barbarous as that of botany: the description of this plant by Linnaeus, shall be a proof. The plant he calls "Cyperus Papyrus; Class Triandria; Order Monogynia; Culm three-sided, naked; umbel longer than the involucres; involucels three-leaved, setaceous, longer; spikelets in threes - Egypt, etc. Involucre eight-leaved; general umbel copious, the rays sheathing at the base; partial on very short peduncles; spikelets alternate, sessile; culm leafy at the base; leaves hollow, ensiform." Hear our plain countryman John Gerarde, who describes the same plant: "Papyrus Nilotica, Paper Reed, hath many large flaggie leaves, somewhat triangular and smooth, not much unlike those of cats-taile, rising immediately from a tuft of roots, compact of many strings; amongst the which it shooteth up two or three naked stalkes, square, and rising some six or seven cubits high above the water; at the top whereof there stands a tuft or bundle off chaffie threds, set in comely order, resembling a tuft of floures, but barren and void of seed;" Gerarde's Herbal, p. 40. Which of the two descriptions is easiest to be understood by common sense, either with or without a knowledge of the Latin language? This plant grows in the muddy banks of the Nile, as it requires an abundance of water for its nourishment. <div eID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> Can the flag grow without water? - Parkhurst supposes that the word אחו achu, which we render flag, is the same with that species of reed which Mr. Hasselquist found growing near the river Nile. He describes it (p. 97) as "having scarcely any branches, but numerous leaves, which are narrow, smooth, channelled on the upper surface; and the plant about eleven feet high. The Egyptians make ropes of the leaves. They lay the plant in water, like hemp, and then make good and strong cables of them." As אח ach signifies to join, connect, associate, hence אחי achi, a brother, אחו achu may come from the same root, and have its name from its usefulness in making ropes, cables, etc., which are composed of associated threads, and serve to tie, bind together, etc.
entries.17e2cb0af05ec22025ee1a1d54931bf9064b89ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16209" type="x-p"/> Whilst it is yet in his greenness - We do not know enough of the natural history of this plant to be able to discern the strength of this allusion; but we learn from it that, although this plant be very succulent, and grow to a great size, yet it is short-lived, and speedily withers; and this we may suppose to be in the dry season, or on the retreat of the waters of the Nile. However, Soon Ripe, soon Rotten, is a maxim in horticulture.
entries.663ccdfdc8591e18861e129457602d43c4fcd6c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> So are the paths - The papyrus and the rush flourish while they have a plentiful supply of ooze and water; but take these away, and their prosperity is speedily at an end; so it is with the wicked and profane; their prosperity is of short duration, however great it may appear to be in the beginning. Thou also, O thou enemy of God, hast flourished for a time; but the blast of God is come upon thee, and now thou art dried up from the very roots. <div eID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16211" type="x-p"/> The hypocrite's hope shall perish - A hypocrite, or rather profligate, has no inward religion, for his heart is not right with God; he has only hope, and that perishes when he gives up the ghost. This is the first place in which the word hypocrite occurs, or the noun חנף chaneph, which rather conveys the idea of pollution and defilement than of hypocrisy. A hypocrite is one who only carries the mask of godliness, to serve secular purposes; who wishes to be taken for a religionist, though he is conscious he has no religion. Such a person cannot have hope of any good, because he knows he is insincere: but the person in the text has hope; therefore hypocrite cannot be the meaning of the original word. But all the vile, the polluted, and the profligate have hope; they hope to end their iniquities before they end life; and they hope to get at last to the kingdom of heaven. Hypocrite is a very improper translation of the Hebrew.
entries.596e4c14b60be5fac3817d06b3a3f35df8c55d25: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16212" type="x-p"/> Whose hope shall be cut off - Such persons, subdued by the strong habits of sin, hope on fruitlessly, till the last thread of the web of life is cut off from the beam; and then they find no more strength in their hope than is in the threads of the spider's web. Mr. Good renders, Thus shall their support rot away. The foundation on which they trust is rotten, and by and by the whole superstructure of their confidence shall tumble into ruin.
entries.572fa3cc9c7b198cafc36c3b12949c668435cc5c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16213" type="x-p"/> He shall lean upon his house - This is all allusion to the spider. When he suspects his web, here called his house, to be frail or unsure, he leans upon it in different parts, propping himself on his hinder legs, and pulling with his fore claws, to see if all be safe. If he find any part of it injured, he immediately adds new cordage to that part, and attaches it strongly to the wall. When he finds all safe and strong, he retires into his hole at one corner, supposing himself to be in a state of complete security, when in a moment the brush or the besom sweeps away both himself, his house, and his confidence. This I have several times observed; and it is in this that the strength and point of the comparison consist. The wicked, whose hope is in his temporal possessions strengthens and keeps his house in repair; and thus leans on his earthly supports; in a moment, as in the case of the spider, his house is overwhelmed by the blast of God's judgments, and himself probably buried in its ruins. This is a very fine and expressive metaphor, which not one of the commentators that I have seen has ever discovered.
entries.875e82c44f33b44fa4ad06c2bbdbaf122bed6b7c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16214" type="x-p"/> He is green before the sun - This is another metaphor. The wicked is represented as a luxuriant plant, in a good soil, with all the advantages of a good situation; well exposed to the sun; the roots intervolving themselves with stones, so as to render the tree more stable; but suddenly a blast comes, and the tree begins to die. The sudden fading of its leaves, etc., shows that its root is become as rottenness, and its vegetable life destroyed. I have often observed sound and healthy trees, which were flourishing in all the pride of vegetative health, suddenly struck by some unknown and incomprehensible blast, begin to die away, and perish from the roots. I have seen also the prosperous wicked, in the inscrutable dispensations of the Divine providence, blasted, stripped, made bare, and despoiled, in the same way.
entries.8fcdc151d1c2b542b480f6330ab4b70cc96e267d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16215" type="x-p"/> If he destroy him from his place - Is not this a plain reference to the alienation of his inheritance? God destroys him from it; it becomes the property of another; and on his revisiting it, the place, by a striking prosopopoeia, says, "I know thee not; I have never seen thee." This also have I witnessed; I looked on it, felt regret, received instruction, and hasted away.
entries.75f7433722ca48001ef938fcfa8a55c03fbcc28f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> Behold this is the joy of his way - A strong irony. Here is the issue of all his mirth, of his sports, games, and pastimes! See the unfeeling, domineering, polluting and polluted scape-grace, levelled with those whom he had despised, a servant of servants, or unable to work through his debaucheries, cringing for a morsel of bread, or ingloriously ending his days in that bane of any well-ordered and civilized state, a parish workhouse. This also I have most literally witnessed. <div eID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16217" type="x-p"/> Out of the earth shall others gross - As in the preceding case, when one plant or tree is blasted or cut down, another may be planted in the same place; so, when a spendthrift has run through his property, another possesses his inheritance, and grows up from that soil in which he himself might have continued to flourish, had it not been for his extravagance and folly. This verse Mr. Good applies to God himself, with no advantage to the argument, nor elucidation of the sense, that I can see. I shall give his translation, and refer to his learned notes for his vindication of the version he has given: - "Behold the Eternal (הוא) exulting in his course; <div eID="gen16217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> Even over his dust shall raise up another." <div eID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16219" type="x-p"/> In this way none of the ancient versions have understood the passage. I believe it to be a strong irony, similar to that which some think flowed from the pen of the same writer: Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth; and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes. But know thou, that for all these God will bring thee into judgment; <reference osisRef="Ecc.11.9">Ecc 11:9</reference>. These two places illustrate each other.
entries.291e9cbfb6de2ce272aa6ab9b8155d2b672ba5a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16220" type="x-p"/> Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man - This is another of the maxims of the ancients, which Bildad produces: "As sure as he will punish and root out the wicked, so surely will he defend and save the righteous."
entries.67bbbcb2094d6fa9460406d18b31ce0e68bfd232: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16221" type="x-p"/> Till he fill thy mouth with laughing - Perhaps it may be well to translate after Mr. Good "Even yet may he fill thy mouth with laughter!" The two verses may be read as a prayer; and probably they were thus expressed by Bildad, who speaks with less virulence than his predecessor, though with equal positiveness in respect to the grand charge, viz., If thou wert not a sinner of no mean magnitude, God would not have inflicted such unprecedented calamities upon thee. This most exceptionable position, which is so contrary to matter of fact, was founded upon maxims which they derived from the ancients. Surely observation must have, in numberless instances, corrected this mistake. They must have seen many worthless men in high prosperity, and many of the excellent of the earth in deep adversity and affliction; but the opposite was an article of their creed, and all appearances and facts must take its colouring. Job's friends must have been acquainted, at least, with the history of the ancient patriarchs; and most certainly they contained facts of an opposite nature. Righteous Abel was persecuted and murdered by his wicked brother, Cain. Abram was obliged to leave his own country on account of worshipping the true God; so all tradition has said. Jacob was persecuted by his brother Esau; Joseph was sold into slavery by his brothers; Moses was obliged to flee from Egypt, and was variously tried and afflicted, even by his own brethren. Not to mention David, and almost all the prophets. All these were proofs that the best of men were frequently exposed to sore afflictions and heavy calamities; and it is not by the prosperity or adversity of men in this world, that we are to judge of the approbation or disapprobation of God towards them. In every case our Lord's rule is infallible: By their fruits ye shall know them.  <chapter eID="Job.8"/> <div eID="gen16221" type="x-p"/>

entries.33b0480221be52bd5fac446a8d634aea97a2b503: <reference osisRef="Job.8.1-Job.4.1">Job 8:1-4   1</reference>  Then began Bildad the Shuhite, and said:   2  How long wilt thou utter such things, <div eID="gen7135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7136" type="x-p"/> And the words of thy mouth are a boisterous wind?   3  Will God reverse what is right, <div eID="gen7136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> Or the Almighty reverse what is just?   4  When thy children sinned against Him, <div eID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7138" type="x-p"/> He gave them over to the hand of their wickedness. <div eID="gen7138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> Bildad<note placement="foot">Nothing can be said respecting the signification of the name בּלדּד even as a probable meaning, unless perhaps = בל־דד, <hi type="italic">sine mammis</hi>, i.e., brought up without his mother’s milk.</note> begins harshly and self-confidently with <hi type="italic">quousque tandem,</hi> עד־אן instead of the usual עד־אנה. אלּה, not: this, but: of this kind, of such kind, as <reference osisRef="Job.12.3">Job 12:3</reference>; Job 16:2. כּבּיר רוּח is poetical, equivalent to גּדולה רוּח, <reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>; רוּח is <hi type="italic">gen. comm.</hi> in the signification wind as well as spirit, although more frequently <hi type="italic">fem.</hi> than <hi type="italic">masc</hi>. He means that Job’s speeches are like the wind in their nothingness, and like a boisterous wind in their vehemence. Bildad sees the justice of God, the Absolute One, which ought to be universally acknowledged, impugned in them. In order not to say directly that Job’s children had died such a sudden death on account of their sin, he speaks conditionally. If they have sinned, death is just the punishment of their sin. God has not arbitrarily swept them away, but has justly given them over to the destroying hand of their wickedness, - a reference to the prologue which belongs inseparably to the whole.
entries.7ab89552185f286c35e596ec59cd245e4d060203: <reference osisRef="Job.8.5-Job.7.5">Job 8:5-7   5</reference>  If thou seekest unto God, <div eID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7140" type="x-p"/> And makest supplication to the Almighty,   6  If thou art pure and upright; Surely! <div eID="gen7140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7141" type="x-p"/> He will care for thee, <div eID="gen7141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7142" type="x-p"/> And restore the habitation of thy righteousness;   7  And if thy beginning was small, <div eID="gen7142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7143" type="x-p"/> Thy end shall be exceeding great. <div eID="gen7143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7144" type="x-p"/> There is still hope for Job (אתּה, in opposition to his children), if, turning humbly to God, he shows that, although not suffering undeservedly, he is nevertheless pure and upright in his inmost mind. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.8.6">Job 8:6</reference></hi> is so intended; not as Mercier and others explain: <hi type="italic">si in posterum puritati et justitiae studueris</hi>. אל־אל שׁחר, to turn one’s self to God earnestly seeking, <hi type="italic">constr. praegnans,</hi> like אל־אל דּרשׁ, Job 5:8. Then begins the conclusion with כּי־עתּה, like Job 13:18. “The habitation of thy righteousness” is Job’s household cleansed and justified from sin. God will restore that; שׁלּם might also signify, give peace to, but restore is far more appropriate. Completely falling back on שׁלם, the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> signifies to recompense, off like being returned for like, and to restore, of a complete covering of the loss sustained. God will not only restore, but increase beyond measure, what Job was and had. The <hi type="italic">verb. masc.</hi> after אחרית here is remarkable. But we need not, with Olsh., read ישׂגּה: we may suppose, with Ewald, according to 174, <hi type="italic">e</hi>, that אהרית is purposely treated as <hi type="italic">masc</hi>. It would be a mistake to refer to <reference osisRef="Prov.23.32">Pro 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.21">Pro 29:21</reference>, in support of it.
entries.004ccb95d969dbfba02f68e56e2bf97709d426d2: Job 8:8-10   8  For inquire only of former ages, <div eID="gen7144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7145" type="x-p"/> And attend to the research of their fathers -   9  For we are of yesterday, without experience, <div eID="gen7145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7146" type="x-p"/> Because our days upon earth are a shadow - 10  Shall they not teach thee, speak to thee, <div eID="gen7146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7147" type="x-p"/> And bring forth words from their heart? <div eID="gen7147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7148" type="x-p"/> This challenge calls <reference osisRef="Deut.32.7">Deu 32:7</reference> to mind. לבּך is to be supplied to כּונן; the conjecture of Olshausen, וּבונן, is good, but unnecessary. רשׁון is after the Aramaic form of writing, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job 15:7</reference>, where this and the ordinary form are combined. The “research of their fathers,” i.e., which the fathers of former generations have bequeathed to them, is the collective result of their research, the profound wisdom of the ancients gathered from experience. Our ephemeral and shadowy life is not sufficient for passing judgment on the dealings of God; we must call history and tradition to our aid. We are תּמול (<hi type="italic">per aphaeresin</hi>, the same as אתמול), yesterday = of yesterday; it is not necessary to read, with Olshausen, מתּמול. There is no occasion for us to suppose that <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference> is an antithesis to the long duration of life of primeval man. לב (<reference osisRef="Job.8.10">Job 8:10</reference>) is not the antithesis of mouth; but has the pregnant signification of a feeling, i.e., intelligent heart, as we find לבב אישׁ, a man of heart, i.e., understanding, <reference osisRef="Job.34.10">Job 34:10</reference>, Job 34:34. יוציאוּ, <hi type="italic">promunt</hi>, calls to mind Mat 13:52. Now follow familiar sayings of the ancients, not directly quoted, but the wisdom of the fathers, which Bildad endeavours to reproduce.
entries.aea2f3ec5539f3e651dd49ba73747546104fd238: Job 8:11-15 11  Doth papyrus grow up without mire? <div eID="gen7148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7149" type="x-p"/> Doth the reed shoot up without water? 12  It is still in luxuriant verdure, when it is not cut off, <div eID="gen7149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7150" type="x-p"/> Then before all other grass it with 13  So is the way of all forgetters of God, <div eID="gen7150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7151" type="x-p"/> And the hope of the ungodly perisheth, 14  Because his hope is cut off, <div eID="gen7151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7152" type="x-p"/> And his trust is a spider’s house: 15  He leaneth upon his house and it standeth not, <div eID="gen7152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7153" type="x-p"/> He holdeth fast to it and it endureth not. <div eID="gen7153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7154" type="x-p"/> Bildad likens the deceitful ground on which the prosperity of the godless stands to the dry ground on which, only for a time, the papyrus or reed finds water, and grows up rapidly: shooting up quickly, it withers as quickly; as the papyrus plant,<note placement="foot">Vid., Champollion-Figeac, <hi type="italic">Aegypten</hi>, German translation, pp. 47f.</note> if it has no perpetual water, though the finest of grasses, withers off when most luxuriantly green, before it attains maturity. גּמא, which, excepting here, is found only in connection with Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.3">Exo 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Isa.35.7">Isa 35:7</reference>, with the general קנה as specific name for reed), is the proper papyrus plant (Cypeerus papyyrus, L.): this name for it is suitably derived in the Hebrew from גּמא, to suck up (comp. Lucan, iv. 136: <hi type="italic">conseritur bibulâ Memphytis cymba papyro</hi>); but is at the same time Egyptian, since Coptic <hi type="italic">kam , cham ,</hi> signifies the reed, and <hi type="italic">'gôm , 'gōme</hi>, a book (like <hi type="italic">liber</hi>, from the bark of a tree).<note placement="foot">Comp. the <hi type="italic">Book of the Dead</hi> (Todtenbuch), ch. 162: “Chapter on the creation of warmth at the back of the head of the deceased. Words over a young cow finished in pure gold. Put them on the neck of the dead, and paint them also on a new papyrus,” etc. Papyrus is here <hi type="italic">cama</hi>: the word is determined by papyrus-roll, fastening and writing, and its first consonant corresponds to the Coptic aspirated g. Moreover, we cannot omit to mention that this <hi type="italic">cama</hi> = <hi type="italic">gôme</hi> also signifies a garment, as in a prayer: “O my mother Isis, come and veil me in thy <hi type="italic">cama</hi>.” Perhaps both ideas are represented in <hi type="italic">volumen</hi>, <hi type="italic">involucrum</hi>; it is, however, also possible that goome is to be etymologically separated from <hi type="italic">kam</hi>, <hi type="italic">cham</hi> = גמא.</note> אחוּ, occurring only in the book of Job and in the history of Joseph, as Jerome (<hi type="italic">Opp. ed. Vallarsi,</hi> iv. 291) learned from the Egyptians, signifies in their language, <hi type="italic">omne quod in palude virem nascitur:</hi> the word is transferred by the lxx into their translation in the form ἄχι (ἄχει), and became really incorporated into the Alexandrian Greek, as is evident from <reference osisRef="Isa.19.7">Isa 19:7</reference> (ערות, lxx καὶ τὸ ἄχι τὸ χλωρόν) and Sir. 40:16 (ἄχι ἐπὶ παντὸς ὕδατος καὶ χείλους ποταμοῦ πρὸ παντὸς χόρτου ἐκτιλήσεται); the Coptic translates <hi type="italic">pi - akhi ,</hi> and moreover <hi type="italic">ake</hi>, <hi type="italic">oke</hi> signify in Coptic <hi type="italic">calamus, juncus.</hi><note placement="foot">The tradition of Jerome, that אחו originally signifies <hi type="italic">viride</hi>, is supported by the corresponding use of the verb in the signification to be green. So in the <hi type="italic">Papyr. Anastas</hi>. No. 3 (in Brugsch, <hi type="italic">Aeg</hi>. Geographic, S. 20, No. 115): <hi type="italic">naif hesbu achach em sim</hi>, his fields are green with herbs; and in a passage in Young, <hi type="italic">Hieroglyphics</hi>, ii. 69: <hi type="italic">achechut uoi aas em senem.t</hi>, the beautiful field is green with senem. The second radical is doubled in <hi type="italic">achech</hi>, as in <hi type="italic">uot-uet</hi>, which certainly signifies <hi type="italic">viriditas</hi>. The substantive is also found represented by three leaf-stalks on one basis; its radical form is <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, plural, weaker or stronger aspirated, <hi type="italic">ahu</hi> or <hi type="italic">akhu</hi>, greenness: comp. Salvolini, <hi type="italic">Campagne dè Rhamsès le Grand</hi>, p. 117; and Brugsch, above, S. 25.</note> יקּטף לא describes its condition: in a condition in which it is not ready for being gathered. By אשׁר, <hi type="italic">quippe, quoniam,</hi> this end of the man who forgets God, and of the חנף, i.e., the secretly wicked, is more particularly described. His hope יקוט, from קטט, or from קוט, <hi type="italic">med. o,</hi><note placement="foot">Both are possible; for even from קטט, the mode of writing, יקוט, is not without numerous examples, as <reference osisRef="Dan.11.12">Dan 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.21">Psa 94:21</reference>; Psa 107:27.</note> in neuter signification <hi type="italic">succiditur</hi>. One would indeed expect a figure corresponding to the spider’s web earlier; and accordingly Hahn, after Reiske, translates: whose hope is a gourd, - an absurd figure, and linguistically impossible, since the gourd or cucumber is קשּׁוּא, which has its cognates in Arabic and Syriac. Saadia<note placement="foot">Vid., Ewald-Dukes’ <hi type="italic">Beiträge zur Gesch. der ältesten Auslegung</hi>, i. 89.</note> translates: whose hope is the thread of the sun. The “thread of the sun” is what we call the <hi type="italic">fliegender Sommer</hi> or <hi type="italic">Altweibersommer,</hi> i.e., the sunny days in the latter months of the year: certainly a suitable figure, but unsupportable by any parallel in language.<note placement="foot">Saadia’s interpretation cannot be supported from the Arabic, for the Arabs call the “<hi type="italic">Altweibersommer</hi>” the deceitful thread (<hi type="italic">el - chaitt el - bâttil</hi>), or “sunslime or spittle” (<hi type="italic">lu‛âb es - schems</hi>), or <hi type="italic">chayta‛ûr</hi> (a word which Ewald, <hi type="italic">Jahrb</hi>. ix. 38, derives from Arab. <hi type="italic">chayt</hi> = יקוט, a word which does not exist, and <hi type="italic">‛ûr</hi>, chaff, a word which is not Arabic), from <hi type="italic">chat‛ara</hi>, to roam about, to be dispersed, to perish, vanish. From this radical signification, <hi type="italic">chaita‛ûr</hi>, like many similar old Arabic words with a fulness of figurative and related meaning, is become an expression for a number of different things, which may be referred to the notion of roaming about and dispersion. Among others, as the Turkish Kamus says, “That thing which on extremely hot days, in the form of a spider’s web, looks as though single threads came down from the atmosphere, which is caused by the thickness of the air,” etc. The form brought forward by Ew., written with Arab. <hi type="italic">t</hi> or <hi type="italic">t̬ ,</hi> is, moreover, a fabrication of our lexicons (Fl.).</note> <div eID="gen7154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7155" type="x-p"/> We must therefore suppose that יקוט, <hi type="italic">succiditur</hi>, first gave rise to the figure which follows: as easily as a spider’s web is cut through, without offering any resistance, by the lightest touch, or a breath of wind, so that on which he depends and trusts is cut asunder. The name for spider’s web, עכּבישׁ בּית,<note placement="foot">The spider is called עכבישׁ, for ענכבישׁ, Arabic <hi type="italic">‛ancabuth</hi>, for which they say <hi type="italic">‛accabuth</hi> in <hi type="italic">Saida</hi>, on ancient Phoenician ground, as <hi type="italic">atta</hi> (thou) for <hi type="italic">anta</hi> (communicated by Wetzstein).</note> leads to the description of the prosperity of the ungodly by בּית (<reference osisRef="Job.8.15">Job 8:15</reference>): His house, the spider’s house, is not firm to him. Another figure follows: the wicked in his prosperity is like a climbing plant, which grows luxuriantly for a time, but suddenly perishes.
